course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Transoceanic Interconnections
unit.description: Study how new maritime technology, state-sponsored voyages, the Columbian Exchange, and coerced labor connected the world's oceans and reshaped societies.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why Portugal sought a sea route to Asia?

To trade for spices without paying Venetian and Ottoman middlemen
To escape the spread of the plague in western Europe

questions.explanation: A direct sea route let Portugal bypass the merchants who controlled the spice trade.
choiceExplanations: Mongol rule had ended long before; middlemen, not closed roads, were the issue.
A direct sea route let Portugal bypass the merchants who controlled the spice trade.
The plague does not explain the voyages.
Portugal sought trade, not farmland, in Asia.
questions.distinguisher: Spices were the goal, but the Mongol Empire had long since broken up; the problem was the profit taken by middlemen.

questions.prompt: According to mercantilism, a state grows wealthy mainly by
choices: exporting more than it imports and gathering precious metals
removing all restrictions on trade
importing more goods than it exports
exporting more than it imports and avoiding the expense of overseas colonies

choices: Bartolomeu Dias
Ferdinand Magellan
Vasco da Gama

choiceExplanations: Dias rounded Africa's tip in 1488 but turned back.

questions.prompt: The voyage of Magellan's expedition from 1519 to 1522 demonstrated that
choices: the oceans were connected and Asia lay just west of Europe
the world's oceans were connected and the Americas lay between Europe and Asia
the world was round, which no educated European had believed
a northwest passage connected the Atlantic and Pacific
questions.explanation: Sailing around the world showed how the oceans linked and where the Americas lay.
choiceExplanations: The voyage revealed the vast Pacific between the Americas and Asia.
Sailing around the world showed how the oceans linked and where the Americas lay.
Educated Europeans already knew the earth was round.

questions.distinguisher: The oceans were connected, but the voyage showed a huge ocean and two continents between Europe and Asia.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, which of the following was a motive for Portuguese voyages?
choices: Reaching sources of gold without Muslim middlemen
Finding farmland for Portuguese settlers in Asia
Escaping religious persecution in Portugal
Reaching sources of silver in the Americas
questions.explanation: Henry sought West African gold without going through North African middlemen.
choiceExplanations: Henry sought West African gold without going through North African middlemen.
The voyages sought trade, not farmland.
The passage does not mention persecution.
The passage concerns Africa and Asia.
questions.distinguisher: The Portuguese sought precious metal, but in Africa; the American silver trade belonged to Spain.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.2 key concept: new state-supported transoceanic maritime exploration occurred in this period, led at first by Portugal
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing Portuguese exploration, 1415–1500
stimulusBlocks.text:
In the early 1400s, Prince Henry of Portugal sponsored voyages down the West African coast. His motives combined a search for gold, a desire to reach Africa's gold-producing regions without going through Muslim middlemen in North Africa, crusading zeal, and curiosity about the coast. The Portuguese crown claimed a share of the profits.

Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488. Ten years later, Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in India, opening a sea route that bypassed the Venetian and Ottoman middlemen who had controlled the spice trade into Europe.

questions.prompt: Vasco da Gama's voyage of 1498 most directly affected the spice trade by
choices: giving Portugal control of spice production in India
creating a land route through the Ottoman Empire
creating a sea route that bypassed Venetian and Ottoman middlemen
ending all of the spice trade that passed through the Mediterranean
questions.explanation: The sea route let Portugal buy spices without going through Venice or the Ottomans.
choiceExplanations: Portugal traded for spices but did not control production in India.
Da Gama's route was by sea.
The sea route let Portugal buy spices without going through Venice or the Ottomans.
Mediterranean trade continued.
questions.distinguisher: Mediterranean spice trade continued for decades; the sea route competed with it rather than ending it.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the Treaty of Tordesillas later gave Portugal
choices: its claim to Florida
its claim to Brazil
its claim to the Philippines
control of Mexico

choiceExplanations: Florida was claimed by Spain.
The line placed eastern South America on the Portuguese side, giving Portugal Brazil.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.2 key concept: Spanish sponsorship of the first Columbian and subsequent voyages across the Atlantic and Pacific dramatically increased European interest in transoceanic travel and trade
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing Spanish exploration, 1492–1522
stimulusBlocks.text:
Christopher Columbus, a Genoese navigator, sailed for the Spanish monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492, hoping to reach Asia by sailing west. Instead he reached the Caribbean. In 1494 the Treaty of Tordesillas divided newly claimed lands outside Europe between Spain and Portugal along a line in the Atlantic, which later gave Portugal its claim to Brazil.

From 1519 to 1522 an expedition led at first by Ferdinand Magellan sailed around the world. Magellan was killed in the Philippines, but one ship returned to Spain, proving that the Americas lay between Europe and Asia and that the oceans were connected.

questions.prompt: The return of Magellan's expedition to Spain in 1522 demonstrated that
choices: Asia could be reached in a few weeks by sailing west
the oceans were connected by a route through Africa
the Atlantic and Pacific oceans were connected
a northwest passage existed through North America
questions.explanation: Sailing around the world proved the oceans were linked.
choiceExplanations: The voyage took three years and showed how vast the Pacific was.
The expedition entered the Pacific through a strait in South America.
Sailing around the world proved the oceans were linked.
No northwest passage was found.
questions.distinguisher: The oceans were connected, but the expedition passed the southern tip of South America, not Africa, to reach the Pacific.

choices: competition among Atlantic kingdoms to reach Asian trade
the spread of the plague along Silk Road routes

choiceExplanations: Neither Cabot nor Cartier found a northwest passage.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.2 key concept: northern Atlantic crossings were undertaken under English, French, and Dutch sponsorship, often with the goal of finding alternative sea routes to Asia
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing English, French, and Dutch voyages to North America, 1497–1610
stimulusBlocks.text:
Sailing for England in 1497, John Cabot reached the coast of Newfoundland. French voyages under Jacques Cartier in the 1530s explored the St. Lawrence River. Both searched for a northwest passage to Asia, and neither found one.

What they found instead were rich fishing grounds and a trade in furs with Indigenous peoples. By the early 1600s, French traders in New France and Dutch traders along the Hudson River were exchanging metal tools, cloth, and guns for beaver pelts, which were in high demand in Europe for hats.

questions.prompt: The fur trade described in the passage was driven mainly by
choices: Spanish laws requiring colonists to trap animals
European demand for beaver meat as food
European demand for beaver pelts used in hats
Indigenous demand for European silver
questions.explanation: Beaver pelts were in high demand in Europe for hats.
choiceExplanations: The trade was French and Dutch, not Spanish.
The pelts, not the meat, drove the trade.
Beaver pelts were in high demand in Europe for hats.
Indigenous traders sought metal tools, cloth, and guns.
questions.distinguisher: Beavers were hunted for their pelts, which made fashionable felt hats.
